episodes.title: A projectile, solved one axis at a time
episodes.question: A drone starts at the origin with velocity (6, 8) m/s and constant acceleration (0, -10) m/s^2. Where is it, and what is its velocity, after 1 s?
episodes.solution: Use r = r0 + v0 t + 1/2 a t^2 and v = v0 + a t component by component. The horizontal motion has zero acceleration; the vertical component changes under gravity. Keep the sign convention explicit.
episodes.visual_hook: Split the screen into x and y motion, then recombine both components into one moving dot and velocity arrow.
episodes.misconception: Gravity changes the vertical velocity here, not the horizontal velocity.

episodes.title: Why 3 m east plus 4 m north is not 7 m
episodes.question: A student walks 3 m east, then 4 m north. Why is the displacement magnitude 5 m rather than 7 m?
episodes.answer: The two perpendicular components form a right triangle, so the displacement magnitude is sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = 5 m. The path length is 7 m; displacement is the straight vector from start to finish.
episodes.solution: Draw the two directed steps tip-to-tail. Distinguish total path length from the magnitude of the net displacement vector, then use the Pythagorean theorem.
episodes.visual_hook: Let a 3-4-5 right triangle assemble from two walking paths while the path-length and displacement labels diverge.
episodes.misconception: Path length and displacement are different quantities, even when both use metres.

episodes.title: When does a dropped stone reach the ground?
episodes.question: A stone is released from rest 45 m above the ground. Taking g = 10 m/s^2 and neglecting air resistance, when does it hit, and what is its velocity just before impact?
episodes.answer: It hits after 3 s with velocity 30 m/s downward.
episodes.solution: Choose upward as positive: y0 = 45 m, v0 = 0, a = -10 m/s^2. Solve 0 = 45 - 5t^2 for the positive time t = 3 s, then v = -10(3) = -30 m/s.
episodes.visual_hook: Track height and velocity together; the height reaches zero as the downward velocity arrow grows.
episodes.misconception: A negative velocity sign gives direction relative to the chosen axis; speed itself is not negative.

episodes.title: Read motion from a velocity-time graph
episodes.question: On a velocity-time graph, what does the slope tell you, and what does signed area tell you?
episodes.answer: Slope is acceleration. Signed area over a time interval is displacement; areas below the time axis count negatively for the chosen positive direction.
episodes.solution: Compare units: (m/s)/s = m/s^2 for slope and (m/s)s = m for area. A negative velocity contributes negative displacement, not negative distance.
episodes.visual_hook: Tilt a velocity-time graph so its slope becomes a visible acceleration arrow, then shade signed areas with opposite directions.
episodes.misconception: Area below the time axis is negative displacement, not negative distance.

episodes.title: A ball thrown upward after one second
episodes.question: A ball leaves a player's hand at 20 m/s upward. With g = 10 m/s^2 downward, where is it after 1 s, and how fast is it moving?
episodes.answer: It is 15 m above the release point and still moving upward at 10 m/s.
episodes.solution: Take upward as positive. At t = 1 s, y - y0 = 20(1) - 1/2(10)(1)^2 = 15 m and v = 20 - 10(1) = 10 m/s.
episodes.visual_hook: Show the upward velocity arrow shrink while the ball continues upward; separate position from velocity.
episodes.misconception: The ball is still moving upward after one second; its downward acceleration has not reversed its velocity yet.

episodes.title: The wall pushes back
episodes.question: When you push a wall, what is the reaction force, and why do the two forces not cancel on you?
episodes.answer: The wall pushes on you with an equal-magnitude, opposite-direction contact force. Your push acts on the wall; the wall's force acts on you, so they act on different objects.
episodes.solution: Draw one force diagram for the person and one for the wall. Only forces on the same chosen object can be summed in that object's net force.
episodes.visual_hook: Separate person and wall into two free-body diagrams; animate the equal-and-opposite contact arrows on different bodies.
episodes.misconception: The action-reaction pair acts on different objects, so it is not a pair of forces on one free-body diagram.

episodes.title: Two carts stick together
episodes.question: A 2 kg cart moving at 3 m/s hits and sticks to a 1 kg cart initially at rest. What is their shared speed just after impact, and how much kinetic energy is lost?
episodes.answer: The carts move at 2 m/s. Initial kinetic energy is 9 J and final kinetic energy is 6 J, so 3 J of kinetic energy is transformed into other forms.
episodes.solution: For the two-cart system with negligible external impulse, (2)(3) + (1)(0) = (2 + 1)v, giving v = 2 m/s. The initial kinetic energy is 9 J; the final kinetic energy is 1/2(3)(2^2) = 6 J. Thus 3 J of kinetic energy is transformed into internal energy, sound, and deformation.
episodes.visual_hook: Animate momentum bars before and after; preserve total momentum while visibly reducing the kinetic-energy bar.
episodes.misconception: Momentum is conserved for the isolated two-cart system; kinetic energy is not conserved in this sticking collision.

episodes.title: When is momentum conserved?
episodes.question: Why can two colliding carts conserve total momentum even though each cart changes its own momentum?
episodes.answer: The carts exert internal forces on each other. For the combined system, those internal impulses cancel; total momentum stays constant when the net external impulse is zero or negligible.
episodes.solution: Draw a boundary around both carts, identify external forces and their impulse over the short collision, and compare total momentum of the combined system before and after.
episodes.visual_hook: Move the system boundary from one cart to both carts; internal impulse arrows disappear from the combined-system ledger.
episodes.misconception: Momentum conservation applies to the defined system when net external impulse is negligible, not automatically to each object.

episodes.title: How fast after a 5 m fall?
episodes.question: A 1 kg object starts from rest 5 m above the ground. If g = 10 m/s^2 and air resistance is negligible, what is its speed just before reaching the ground?
episodes.solution: The lost gravitational potential energy mgh becomes kinetic energy: mgh = 1/2 mv^2. Mass cancels, so v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(100) = 10 m/s.
episodes.visual_hook: Transform a height bar into a speed arrow while the total mechanical-energy bar remains constant.
episodes.misconception: The mass cancels in this idealized energy equation, so the predicted speed does not depend on the object's mass.

episodes.title: Where does kinetic energy go when carts stick?
episodes.question: If total energy is conserved, why does the kinetic energy decrease when two carts collide and stick?
episodes.answer: Kinetic energy is not conserved in a perfectly inelastic collision. Some mechanical energy becomes internal energy, sound, and deformation; total energy for a sufficiently complete system remains conserved.
episodes.solution: Track the system's energy forms rather than treating kinetic energy as the only energy. Keep the momentum and energy claims separate: momentum can be conserved while kinetic energy changes.
episodes.visual_hook: Show kinetic-energy bars shrinking as internal-energy, sound, and deformation indicators grow; keep a total-energy outline fixed.
episodes.misconception: Conservation of total energy does not imply conservation of kinetic energy by itself.
